You eat Hesper's onion stew standing, then drag a stool to the bedside. She props Piper on a rolled blanket without a word, and she lays a second stool by the door where she can see you, in case she is needed.

Medicine (14): with an hour of watching, the picture clears. His lips are dry but not blue, his fingernails are pink, and the phlegm in the basin is thick yellow and not streaked with red. The fever is real, hot and dry to the touch, but his breathing, though wet, is steady and even. This is a lung-fever from a chill that settled low, the kind that strikes a boy who has spent too many nights on a cart. It is not the Grey Fever you grew up among. It is not likely to spread. Most important, it can be borne if he is kept upright, warm, and wet-lipped with broth.

You bathe his brow and wrists with a cool damp cloth, change it every hour, and prop him as Hesper did. You hum Edda's hymn low, over and over. Around ten the fever turns. Around eleven he opens his eyes, looks at the strange man on the stool, says "Is Da back?" in a cracked whisper, and falls asleep again before you can answer.

He was orphaned at six when the Grey Fever emptied the houses along the water, and was raised by the temple's old healer, Mother Edda Thorne, who died last winter of old age and left him her plain wooden amulet. He keeps a promise to carry her work to places that have no healer at all. His past (true and not to be contradicted): as a child he sat beside dying neighbors because Edda had too few hands; the night she told him to leave a dying fisherman and rest, he refused, and the man's daughter later thanked him, which is the root of his stubbornness. He hums hymns while he works, is warm and patient, and swore never to let anyone suffer alone again. He is inflexible in his thinking. Something has just happened that needs him: a frightened child or farmer hurries out to flag him down, begging for help for sick or wounded people sheltering in a barn, where the trouble is more than illness alone (for example, injuries from a recent attack by raiders or wild beasts, with the threat possibly still near). entries.text: notebook: updated Piper

You eat quickly. Hesper's onion soup and bread are hot and good. Then you bring the stool in, and Hesper props Piper's shoulders with a rolled blanket without being asked. She says, gruffly, "I'll leave the door ajar." You keep the kettle at a low steam and hum Edda's hymn under your breath.

Yes, he has a fever, and you can work on it. A cloth wrung in cool water laid on his brow and wrists, changed every little while, eases the flush. His skin is hot and dry to the touch, but not scorching.

You try Medicine again, taking real time over it. Medicine (8): the second reading is no clearer than the first. His lips are dry and cracked but not blue, which is a good sign. The phlegm in the basin is thick and yellow-gray, and his chest is still muddy to the ear. None of it tells you whether this is a chill that will break on its own or a deeper rot in the lung. Both fit. You can't be sure, and I won't pretend otherwise. I can tell you plainly that nothing here looks magical or unnatural, and nothing suggests he is in immediate danger tonight. Cure Wounds won't help, since it mends wounds and not fever. The remedy is time, fluids, steam, and keeping him propped.

Two hours pass. Piper sleeps more easily, and his breathing loosens a little under the steam. It is twenty past nine.

One thing to weigh: if you sit up with him all night, you won't get a long rest, because a long rest needs at least 8 hours of sleep or light activity, with no more than 2 hours of watch. You could sit the first hours and then sleep on the pallet at his side, or sleep fully and let Hesper wake you if he changes. Your spells are all still ready, and you'd want them back before Greywater.

Before you leave, you look in on the east lane one last time. Tessa is feeding. Ilsa meets you at the door with the baby on her shoulder and a face that is no longer gray. Osric has already changed his dressing and sends Wren's mother up with a skein of undyed wool as thanks, which Wren's mother presses on you with a shy smile. Perrin Gale is sitting on his stool at the vat when you pass, and he lifts one hand without a word.

Wren wakes as you gather your pack. You give her the letter for Mother Aldith, and she holds it against her chest. Her mother, a broad woman with stained arms, has come to the chapel door and listens, frowning, while you explain. She does not say yes and she does not say no. She says, "Bring word back from the bonesetter first. Then we'll see." It is a fair answer.

The road to Stonebridge runs along the river, through rolling pasture and orchard, a day's walk. Morning mist is lifting off the water. You walk into the new sun with the loaf nearly gone, Maud's honey in your pack, and the memory of five lives mended by plain hands and a few prayers.

You wake at 4:50, long before the light, to the smell of cold stone and the sound of Wren breathing on the bench with her basket still in her lap. Prayers, slots, and Channel Divinity are all restored. Your list stays as you chose it: Healing Word, Shield of Faith, Guiding Bolt, Sanctuary, and Protection from Evil and Good, with Bless and Cure Wounds always ready. You are at 17 of 17 HP, with three first-level slots.

You kneel at the altar a while in the dark and hum as the sky greys. Wren wakes with a start and a guilty look, and you tell her it is no sin to sleep in a chapel. She presses the letter into her apron pocket and walks you to the village edge. Behind her, Osric stands at his shed door with his arm in a clean dressing, and he lifts the good hand to you. A thin line of smoke rises from Ilsa's chimney.

The valley road to Stonebridge runs south along the river, a day's walk. You take it at a steady pace through the morning mist, past the dye racks and the weir and out into pasture. The sun comes up behind you as you go.

sheet.name: Brannoc Ashdown
sheet.opening: Brannoc Ashdown, a young human cleric of the Life domain, has been on the road only a few weeks, walking out from Millbrook Landing, the little river town of fishermen and reed-cutters where he grew up. He was orphaned at six when the Grey Fever emptied the houses along the water, and was raised by the temple's old healer, Mother Edda Thorne, who died last winter of old age and left him her plain wooden amulet. He keeps a promise to carry her work to places that have no healer at all. His past (true and not to be contradicted): as a child he sat beside dying neighbors because Edda had too few hands; the night she told him to leave a dying fisherman and rest, he refused, and the man's daughter later thanked him, which is the root of his stubbornness. He hums hymns while he works, is warm and patient, and swore never to let anyone suffer alone again. He is inflexible in his thinking. Open play on a muddy back road at dusk, at the edge of a small, struggling settlement with no priest or healer, its few lanterns lit early and its doors shut. Something has just happened that needs him: a frightened child or farmer hurries out to flag him down, begging for help for sick or wounded people sheltering in a barn, where the trouble is more than illness alone (for example, injuries from a recent attack by raiders or wild beasts, with the threat possibly still near). Brannoc has his mace, chain mail, shield, light crossbow, priest's pack, and 15 gp. Give him a clear, immediate call to act, and room to choose between healing, protecting, and investigating.

features: Divine Domain: Choose one domain related to your deity, such as Life. Each domain is detailed at the end of the class description, and each one provides examples of gods associated with it. Your choice grants you domain spells and other features when you choose it at 1st level. It also grants you additional ways to use Channel Divinity when you gain that feature at 2nd level, and additional benefits at 6th, 8th, and 17th levels.

Domain Spells: Each domain has a list of spells--its domain spells--that you gain at the cleric levels noted in the domain description. Once you gain a domain spell, you always have it prepared, and it doesn't count against the number of spells you can prepare each day. If you have a domain spell that doesn't appear on the cleric spell list, the spell is nonetheless a cleric spell for you.
Bonus Proficiency: When you choose this domain at 1st level, you gain proficiency with heavy armor.

Disciple of Life: Also starting at 1st level, your healing spells are more effective. Whenever you use a spell of 1st level or higher to restore hit points to a creature, the creature regains additional hit points equal to 2 + the spell's level.

Channel Divinity (1/rest): At 2nd level, you gain the ability to channel divine energy directly from your deity, using that energy to fuel magical effects. You start with two such effects: Turn Undead and an effect determined by your domain. Some domains grant you additional effects as you advance in levels, as noted in the domain description. When you use your Channel Divinity, you choose which effect to create. You must then finish a short or long rest to use your Channel Divinity again. Some Channel Divinity effects require saving throws. When you use such an effect from this class, the DC equals your cleric spell save DC. Beginning at 6th level, you can use your Channel Divinity twice between rests, and beginning at 18th level, you can use it three times between rests. When you finish a short or long rest, you regain your expended uses.

Channel Divinity: Turn Undead: As an action, you present your holy symbol and speak a prayer censuring the undead. Each undead that can see or hear you within 30 feet of you must make a Wisdom saving throw. If the creature fails its saving throw, it is turned for 1 minute or until it takes any damage. A turned creature must spend its turns trying to move as far away from you as it can, and it can't willingly move to a space within 30 feet of you. It also can't take reactions. For its action, it can use only the Dash action or try to escape from an effect that prevents it from moving. If there's nowhere to move, the creature can use the Dodge action.

Channel Divinity: Preserve Life: Starting at 2nd level, you can use your Channel Divinity to heal the badly injured. As an action, you present your holy symbol and evoke healing energy that can restore a number of hit points equal to five times your cleric level. Choose any creatures within 30 feet of you, and divide those hit points among them. This feature can restore a creature to no more than half of its hit point maximum. You can't use this feature on an undead or a construct. At level 2: 10 hit points to divide.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

line:
I spend the last of the evening kneeling at the plain stone altar, thanking the gods for Piper's mending, Osric's arm, and little Tessa's easy sleep, and humming Edda's hymn until Wren drowses off on the bench with her yarn basket in her lap. Then I lay out my pallet and let the long rest take me.

For tomorrow I'll keep my list as it is: Healing Word, Shield of Faith, Guiding Bolt, Sanctuary, and Protection from Evil and Good, with Bless and Cure Wounds always ready. I'll go down to Stonebridge in the morning to find Mother Aldith for Perrin and Wren, and keep my eyes open for the next place with no healer.

input.add_to_description: Day 5 dawn: Brannoc finished a long rest in the chapel; the village left bread and a small purse of coin (a few silver) on the altar for the road. Wren sleeps on the bench. Road to Stonebridge runs down-valley, a day's walk.

entries.text: notebook: updated Greywater

Sleep takes you in the chapel's quiet, the stone cool at your back and Wren's slow breathing on the bench. Nothing wakes you.

It is a little before five on Day 5, and the long rest is done. You are at 17 of 17 HP with all three slots and Channel Divinity restored, and your Hit Dice are back. Your list stands as you chose it: Healing Word, Shield of Faith, Guiding Bolt, Sanctuary, and Protection from Evil and Good, with Bless and Cure Wounds always ready.

The first gray is in the windows. On the altar, beside Wren's jar of wildflowers, someone has left a heel of fresh bread wrapped in cloth, a wedge of cheese, and a twist of paper with a few silver coins inside, the small gifts of a village that had no one to thank before. The paper is smudged blue at one corner, and you suspect Maud. Wren is awake, sitting up with the letter in both hands. She says nothing, but she looks at you with the whole of her face.

The road to Stonebridge runs down-valley along the river, a day's walk. It is a bonesetter's town with a market, and the first real town you have seen since you left Millbrook Landing. You carry a letter for Mother Aldith, a purse, the Powder, and a promise to Perrin.
